blank_check.what: every written PNG is decoded and its luminance measured; a uniform image is the known Vulkan failure (leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp#1031: blank PNG, exit success)
blank_check.bound: blank when spread <= 2/255 AND stdev <= 1.0, or alpha is 0 everywhere sampled

resume.what: recipe = prompt + negative(if it can act) + size + cfg + steps + seed; a match is skipped, a mismatch is made again
resume.record: made.json 3 item(s); the previous manifest 0 recorded + 0 reconstructed; 3 item(s) on record in total

negatives.what: --negative-prompt is passed whenever an item has one; it only ACTS when cfg != 1.0, because sd-cli evaluates the unconditional branch only then

selection.what: only = the ids asked for by name; limit = how many pictures this run may GENERATE, which skipped items do not count against

images.binds_to: CANDIDATE FOR THE HOOK SHEET'S STREET PANEL - pass 2 of 3, written from pass 1's faults.
images.prompt: the view filling the frame edge to edge, Use case: historical-scene. One photoreal pedestrian eye-height concept panel for LEDGER, the fictional British port town Meridian, a wet overcast working weekday in 1990. THE SUBJECT IS A MINICAB OFFICE AND ITS RANK, and it fills the right half of the frame: MICKEY'S CARS, a small ground-floor MINICAB OFFICE in a red brick terrace - a wide plain plate glass window with a HAND-LETTERED CARD taped inside reading MICKEY'S, a bare counter behind the glass with a two-way RADIO SET and a hardbacked FARE BOOK open on it, a wall clock, a strip light, a couple of moulded plastic chairs against the side wall for people waiting, and a plain painted fascia over the window. THREE ORDINARY DARK SALOON CARS WAIT NOSE TO TAIL AT THE KERB DIRECTLY OUTSIDE IT as a taxi rank, one driver leaning on a wing with his arms folded. THE BAY NEAREST THE CAMERA, on the same side and closer, HAS HAD ITS OLD SHOPFRONT TORN OUT AND REPLACED BY A FLAT ALUMINIUM WINDOW UNIT in the cheap commercial manner of the 1980s: a plain rectangular frame of thin dark metal sections set FLAT against the bare brickwork, metal top to bottom and edge to edge, one wide sheet of plate glass divided by two slim metal glazing bars, a matching flat metal door beside it with a long metal push bar, a cold white fluorescent tube burning inside just behind the glass, cardboard boxes and stacked goods pushed against the window from inside, a PATTERNED GLAZED TILE STALLRISER below the glass, and raw new brick repair patches around the opening where the old front was cut away. Behind and beyond them the street runs on: a continuous two-storey red and soot brick party-wall terrace in repeated 6 m bays under a 35 degree slate roof, party-wall chimney stacks, varied roof heights, flat brick arches over tall narrow white two-over-two sash windows upstairs, and further shop bays whose painted fascia boards are too far off and too rain-streaked for their lettering to be read. 6 m wet asphalt carriageway with a crowned camber, a white centre line, double yellow lines both sides, 2 m stone flag pavement each side with a kerb. HEAVILY WORN AND SOOTED: black soot streaks running down the brick under every gutter and beside every cast iron downpipe, a dark splashed metre at the foot of every wall from pavement splash, flaking paint on the joinery, rust stains, patched pointing - uneven and patchy across the fronts. Two or three ordinary working people at different distances in 1990 British clothes, seen from behind or too far off for a face to read. At the far end the ground rises inland into CONTOUR-FOLLOWING BRICK TERRACES STEPPING UP THE SLOPE BEHIND STONE RETAINING WALLS, pale and soft in the haze.
